#### Why there are three shapes, and why one of them has no answer without a setting

**Fixed (tumbling) windows** partition event time into equal, contiguous, non-overlapping spans. Every event belongs to exactly one, so the 4 window sums here (19, 11, 7, 8) add up to 45 — the whole dataset. They answer "how many per 120s", and they are the shape that reconciles against a batch job.

**Sliding (hopping) windows** are fixed-length but overlapping, defined by a size and a slide — here 120s wide starting every 60s. 6 of the 9 events land in 2 windows at once, so the results total **78** against a dataset of 45. Output volume scales as size / slide = 2×. They answer "what is the rolling 120s figure, refreshed every 60s".

**Session windows** are data-driven: a session is a burst of activity separated from the next by a gap of inactivity — here 120s. At that gap key `a` gets 3 sessions and key `b` gets 2, over the same span of event time, because they were active at different moments. No session has the same length as another and none starts on a round boundary; both facts follow from the boundaries being set by the data.

**And here is the part that is easy to miss.** Sweep the gap over the same stream and key `a`'s session count goes **4 → 3 → 2 → 1** at gaps of 40s, 120s, 130s, 300s. The events never change. Only the definition of "a visit" does.

So "how many sessions did this user have?" has **no answer in the data** until someone states the gap. It is a product definition that happens to live in a config file — which is why the window shape is part of the answer rather than an implementation detail.

#### When to reach for each shape, and what each one costs

**Fixed windows whenever the question names a period.** "Per minute", "per hour", "daily" — the shape is decided and nothing else needs considering. Totals reconcile, state is bounded by (keys × open windows), and a batch job over the same data gives the same answer.

**Sliding windows for a moving measure,** and budget for 2× the output and 2× the state. The trap is comparing their total to the input total: 78 against 45 here, and the overlap is the intent, not a bug.

**Session windows when the boundary is a property of the user's behaviour,** not of the clock — engagement, a visit, a trip, a conversation. Accept that the number of state entries is data-dependent (5 for 9 events here) and cannot be sized in advance.

**Do not reach for sessions to approximate "recent activity".** A sliding window answers that with bounded state and no merging.

**What this does not settle:** session bounds are provisional. A later event can extend a session, which means it can change a value that has already been reported — and at some gap settings that is forced rather than possible. The next concept walks the full lifecycle, and the one after that finds the exact gap at which this stream requires a retraction.

The animation loops through all 4 steps. Expand any step to study it on its own.

<details>
<summary><b>Step 1 of 4</b> — fixed windows partition time: one event, one window</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch04-shapes/frames/step-01.svg" alt="Step 1: fixed windows partition time: one event, one window" width="1040">

Fixed windows are the easy case and the one to reach for by default. Equal length, contiguous, non-overlapping — so each of the 9 events appears exactly once and the 4 sums add to 45. If a question names a period ("per minute", "per hour"), this is the shape, and nothing else needs considering.

</details>
<details>
<summary><b>Step 2 of 4</b> — sliding windows overlap: one event, several windows</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch04-shapes/frames/step-02.svg" alt="Step 2: sliding windows overlap: one event, several windows" width="1040">

Sliding windows answer "the rolling 120s figure, refreshed every 60s". Read the third column: 6 events are in 2 windows, which is why the totals cannot be compared to the input. The first few events are in one window only because event time starts at 12:00 — there is no window before it.

</details>
<details>
<summary><b>Step 3 of 4</b> — session windows are defined by the DATA, not the clock</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch04-shapes/frames/step-03.svg" alt="Step 3: session windows are defined by the DATA, not the clock" width="1040">

Sessions model behaviour rather than counting. Every boundary here was chosen by a silence of more than 120s: key a's first session ends at 12:00:03 because its next activity is 127s later. That is why two users over one time span get 3 and 2 sessions, not the same number.

</details>
<details>
<summary><b>Step 4 of 4</b> — and the gap is part of the ANSWER, not a tuning knob</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch04-shapes/frames/step-04.svg" alt="Step 4: and the gap is part of the ANSWER, not a tuning knob" width="1040">

This is the step that matters most in practice. Key a has 4, 3, 2, 1 sessions at gaps of 40s, 120s, 130s, 300s — four different answers from identical data. The gap is not a performance setting; it is the operational definition of "a visit", and choosing it is the product decision the engineering work is downstream of.

</details>
